issues.issue: The named Licensor is Rank Licensing, Inc., while the notice block in Section 12 directs notices to Hard Rock Cafe International (DEL), Inc.; the identity of the contracting licensor entity could be questioned. The definition in 1(n) covering successors and transferees largely cures this.

The recital asserts flatly that Licensor 'has the right and authority to license' the Marks, whereas the operative warranty in Section 2(a) qualifies ownership as 'subject only to whatever actions or inactions may have been taken ... by Morton'. A dispute over what Licensor actually owned could turn on which text controls.

'All confusingly similar names, marks and logos ... and derivations thereof, to the maximum extent permitted by law' is an open-ended catch-all sitting against the enumerated examples ('Rock Cafe', 'Hard Rock'), leaving the reach of 'Hard Rock Marks' uncertain. Whether a bare 'Hard Rock' usage is a reserved Hard Rock Mark or a licensed Hotel/Casino Mark is genuinely contestable.

The carve-out 'except as expressly provided herein' does not say which provisions expressly provide otherwise, leaving the boundary between Hotel Marks and other Hard Rock Marks unfixed. The definition is otherwise a list-by-exhibit.

Exhibit A, which fixes the Hard Rock Hotel Marks, itself lists 'Hard Rock Casino' — the very mark Exhibit B designates as a Hard Rock Casino Mark under Section 1(c). The two definitions therefore overlap in a way that cannot be fully harmonised.

Exhibit B lists 'Hard Rock Casino', but Exhibit A (defining the Hard Rock Hotel Marks under Section 1(b)) lists the same mark, so a single mark falls in both defined categories despite each definition excluding 'any other Hard Rock Marks'. Provisions keyed to one category or the other (e.g. 2(b)(i)) become uncertain in application.

'An all-inclusive place for lodging, with indoor corridors and offering a variety of amenities' uses undefined and oddly specific criteria — 'all-inclusive' and 'a variety of amenities' have no measurable boundary. Because Section 2(b)(i) and Section 3(a) both turn on whether a facility is a 'Hotel', the vagueness is operative.

'A substantial source of revenue and its principal function' fixes no threshold, so whether a gaming facility qualifies as a 'Casino' is a matter of degree. The riverboat sentence repeats the same undefined 'substantial' standard.

'Immediately adjoining contiguous facility' and, failing that, 'part of the same "Hard Rock" complex/development' set no spatial limit, so whether separated buildings form one Hotel/Casino is contestable. The term controls the Hotel-Marks restriction in 2(b)(i).

A 'Hard Rock Hotel' is defined as a Hotel in the Morton Territories, yet Section 2(b)(i) forbids Licensee from using the Hotel Marks in any Hotel that is not a Hotel/Casino, and Section 3(a) uses the same defined term to describe facilities Licensor may not operate in Nevada. The defined term is deployed inconsistently across the instrument.

The clause contains transcription errors — 'fifty (SO) mile radius form the City Hall' — and measures the radius from 'City Hall or other similarly recognized civic center structure located reasonably near the geographic center', a floating reference point. The Texas/Greater Houston carve-out-within-a-carve-out compounds the imprecision.

'Any and all services provided by Licensee in connection with or relating to the operation of the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos' is boundless at the edges: whether entertainment events, broadcasts or third-party concessions are 'Licensed Services' is genuinely arguable. The definition drives the quality obligations in Section 4(a) and 4(d), so its reach matters.

'Any and all personal property, products and merchandise bearing the ... Marks and offered for sale or sold by Licensee' does not say whether items given away, sold by sublicensees, or sold outside the Territories are Licensed Products. The sale restrictions in 2(b)(iv)-(v) depend on that boundary.

The definition sweeps in 'successors, assigns or transferees' without limit, while Section 3(a) and Section 11(a) impose Licensor-specific prohibitions (e.g. no Hard Rock Hotel in Nevada) whose application to a transferee is not addressed. The point is real but narrow.

The worldwide carve-out — Licensee may 'engage in the promotion, advertising or marketing (not including the sale of merchandise) and broadcasting of the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos ... anywhere in the world' — has no boundary: whether a televised programme or other content is 'promotion ... and broadcasting of' the licensed facilities, as against unlicensed extraterritorial use of the Marks, is squarely contestable. 'Solely in connection with ... promotion of' in the grant sentence carries the same uncertainty.

The grant of an 'exclusive license ... only in the Morton Territories' sits against the second sentence of Section 3(a), which lets Licensor use and exploit the Hard Rock Hotel Marks 'anywhere in the world' for a non-casino Hotel. The two cannot both be given full effect inside the Territories.

The bar on using the Hotel Marks in a Hotel that is not a Hotel/Casino must be squared with Section 2(b)(vii), which contemplates 'other Hard Rock Hotels ... developed, operated, owned, or managed by Licensee', and with the definition of Hard Rock Hotel in 1(g). Read together it is unclear whether Licensee may ever operate a Hard Rock Hotel without a casino.

The modifier is misplaced: 'any restaurant in any Hard Rock Hotel/Casino or Hard Rock Casino, or anywhere else that is confusingly similar to a Hard Rock Cafe restaurant' can be read either as barring all in-facility restaurants or only confusingly similar ones. The following sentence pulls toward the narrower reading but does not resolve the grammar.

'Licensor shall use its best efforts to maintain, protect and preserve such registrations' is an undefined standard, and the trigger for Licensee's self-help — a failure 'reasonably likely to affect' the Marks in the Territories — is equally open. Both would have to be construed before the fallback right could be applied.

Licensor 'shall retain the sole right to apply for' registrations yet 'shall consent to any request by Licensee for Licensor to apply', and the proviso then lets Licensee file as Licensor's agent — a tension with the 'sole right' sentence and with Section 13's disclaimer of agency. Section 13 expressly excepts 2(b)(iii), which mitigates but does not eliminate the friction.

The final sentence excepts only 'clause 2(b)(vii)' from the requirement that Licensed Products 'must always bear the geographic location where sold', but the provision that displaces geographic marking is 2(b)(v) (Internet address as location); the cross-reference appears to be mistaken. What 'the geographic location where sold' means for a product ordered remotely is itself unfixed.

The 'always bear the geographic location' rule cannot be squared with Section 2(b)(v), which permits Internet-sold products to bear the Internet address instead, since 2(b)(iv)'s exception points to a different subsection. One of the two must yield.

The clause allows Internet sales of Licensed Products but does not say whether the buyer's location matters, and 'the Internet address as the Licensed Products' location' is an unusual designation whose sufficiency is arguable. The carve-out 'except for Hard Rock Internet access kits' is undefined.

Permitting worldwide Internet sales sits uneasily with Section 2(a), which confines exploitation of the Marks to the Morton Territories and excludes 'the sale of merchandise' from the worldwide promotion carve-out. Whether Internet sales may reach customers outside the Territories is left unresolved.

'The other designations such as "Beach Club" or "Athletic Club"' is an open class introduced by two examples, so which further designations qualify is uncertain (ejusdem generis). 'The geographic or other designation described herein' compounds the problem by referring to nothing definite.

Exhibit D ('Beach Club / Or Athletic Club') is identical in content to Exhibit E, yet this clause permits continued use of the Exhibit D designations in other Hard Rock facilities while Section 2(b)(viii) requires Licensee to 'forever cease displaying such designations' after eighteen months. The two subsections give opposite answers for the same words.

'To sell whatever merchandise is currently being sold' fixes the permitted inventory by an unrecorded snapshot as of the signing date, with no schedule identifying it. Enforcing the eighteen-month wind-down would require proof of what was 'currently being sold'.

The forever-cease obligation for the Exhibit E designations contradicts Section 2(b)(vii), which permits the Exhibit D designations — the same 'Beach Club'/'Athletic Club' words — to be used in other Hard Rock Hotels and Casinos indefinitely. The exhibits do not distinguish the two sets.

'All rights not specifically granted' turns on how 'specifically granted' is read, and the grant in Section 2(a) is expressed in broad functional language ('use and exploit ... in connection with the development, operation ... and promotion'). The reservation therefore has no determinate residue.

The blanket reservation must be reconciled with Section 9(b), under which Licensee is 'solely entitled to all economic benefits' of the licensed rights, and with the perpetual, royalty-free grant in 9(a). Whether an unenumerated exploitation belongs to Licensor or Licensee is left open.

The sentence first preserves Licensor's rights only 'outside the Morton Territories' and then gives Licensor the Hotel Marks 'anywhere in the world for a Hotel facility that does not include a Casino' — the second limb is on its face wider than the first. The Nevada carve-out implies the wider reading, but the clause does not say so.

Licensor's worldwide right to use the Hard Rock Hotel Marks for non-casino hotels cannot be squared with the 'exclusive license ... only in the Morton Territories' granted to Licensee by Section 2(a). Only the State of Nevada is expressly carved out, leaving the rest of the Territories contested.

The covenant never to attack applies 'during the Term of this Agreement or thereafter', yet Section 9(a) makes the licence perpetual and the Agreement contains no termination mechanism, so 'thereafter' has no referent. This is a loose end rather than a contradiction.

Goodwill inuring 'to the sole benefit of Licensor' sits against Section 9(b), which entitles Licensee 'solely ... to all economic benefits resulting from' the licensed rights. The provisions are probably reconcilable (goodwill versus revenue) but the words overlap.
'Dominate, modify or qualify' the Marks is an undefined and impressionistic test for what added wording is forbidden. Any added word arguably 'qualifies' the mark.

The clause permits added terms 'other than geographical designations' only, yet Sections 2(b)(vi) and 2(b)(vii) expressly allow non-geographic designations such as 'Beach Club' and 'Athletic Club'. The two cannot both be read literally.

The standard — 'good quality at least as high as the quality of similar goods presently sold or distributed by Licensee ... at the Las Vegas Hard Rock Hotel/Casino' — benchmarks quality against an unrecorded 1996 snapshot, and 'quality' of services is not defined to say whether it reaches content, image or tone as opposed to workmanship. Both limbs invite competing readings.

Section 4(f) declares that all standards of operation exist 'solely to ensure the quality of the goods and services' and protect goodwill, which cuts against reading 4(a) as a general control over how Licensee runs its business. The interaction is a live source of dispute.

The sentence is garbled — 'furnish or render to Licensor ... requested Licensed Services, representative samples on the premises of each Licensed Product' — so what Licensee must actually produce, and whether samples leave the premises, is unclear. The list ends with an open 'all other materials' catch-all.

'Wherever the same may be used with reasonable convenience' is an unusual and imprecise trigger for a mandatory marking obligation, and 'the appropriate notice of registration' is not specified. Compliance could not be measured without construing both phrases.

The declaration that Licensor's monitoring rights exist 'solely' for quality and goodwill purposes limits the inspection and approval rights conferred by Sections 4(b) and 4(c) and the supervision powers acknowledged in Section 13. A party could argue 4(f) narrows rights that those clauses grant in unqualified terms.

Arbitration is confined to disputes about 'the failure of Licensee to conform to any provision of quality control as set forth herein', but the Agreement never identifies which provisions are 'provisions of quality control' — Section 4 is headed 'QUALITY, NOTICES, APPROVALS, AND SAMPLES' and other clauses bear on quality too. Whether a given claim is arbitrable therefore turns on construing that phrase.

The clause makes such disputes arbitrable while Section 5(d) excludes everything 'not specifically identified hereinabove' and Section 14 sends all other claims to New York courts; mixed claims must be allocated between the two regimes. Section 11(a)'s promise of court injunctions adds to the overlap.

The arbitrator's power to grant permanent injunctions overlaps Section 11(a), which entitles Licensor to obtain injunctions and specific performance 'from a court of competent jurisdiction'. Which forum controls injunctive relief on a quality-control dispute is not stated.

'Any claims or controversies not specifically identified hereinabove, including but not limited to' validity disputes carves arbitration back by reference to an unstated list, so the excluded class is defined only negatively. The two named examples do not delimit the general words.

The exclusion has to be read against Section 5(a), which sends quality-control disputes to binding arbitration; a claim mixing quality-control breach with trademark validity or enforceability falls on both sides of the line. Section 14's court-forum clause depends on the same boundary.

'Best efforts to protect the ... Marks and the goodwill associated therewith' is undefined and unmeasured, with no benchmark, cost limit or specified conduct. Whether a party's conduct met it could only be resolved by construing the phrase.

A mutual best-efforts duty to protect the Marks and their goodwill is difficult to reconcile with Section 4(f) and Section 13, which state that Licensor's supervisory rights exist solely for quality and goodwill protection, and with Section 6(d)'s allocation of enforcement to each party at its own cost. The overlap is real but not a flat contradiction.

'Any action itself which would affect the ownership of or damage, dilute or modify' the Marks is extremely broad and undefined — almost any use 'affects' or 'modifies' a mark. The provision gives no standard for distinguishing licensed use from prohibited action.

The flat bar on any use of designations 'identical with or confusingly similar to' the Marks, and the closing bar on merchandise bearing 'such designations', cannot be read literally alongside the licence in Section 2(a) and the merchandising permitted by Sections 2(b)(iv)-(v) and 2(b)(vii). The 'only as expressly provided herein in clause 2(b)' proviso does not resolve which merchandise may bear which designation.

The clause first says each party may sue 'at its own cost and expense and any monies recovered will be for the account of such party', then says costs of 'joint proceedings' are borne equally and recoveries divided equally, without defining when a proceeding becomes 'joint'. The two sentences give different answers for the same suit if the other party lends assistance.

The indemnity covers 'any suits, loss and damage arising out of any service or act ... in relation to the Hard Rock Hotel Marks, or the Hard Rock Casino Marks', with no fault requirement, cap or carve-out for Licensor's own conduct. Whether it extends to claims brought by Licensor itself, or to losses caused by Licensor, is unresolved and would be construed against the drafter.

The duty to cross-reference the other party's facilities applies only 'when practical and appropriate', a wholly subjective qualifier that leaves the obligation without an ascertainable content. 'In locations where both parties maintain ... Hard Rock Facilities' is also undefined as to geographic scale.

An agreement 'to discuss the possibility' of mutual sponsorship states no obligation capable of breach — it is an agreement to agree. Any attempt to enforce it would require a court to supply content the clause lacks.

The structure 'Licensor may develop ... a Web page for the Hard Rock Cafe Restaurants, and other Hard Rock Facilities ... except that Licensee may develop ... a Web page for the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos or Casinos in the Morton Territories' does not say whether Licensee's right is exclusive or merely permissive. It is also unclear whether 'in the Morton Territories' limits the facilities covered or the reach of the web page itself.

A worldwide-accessible web page for Territory facilities is hard to square with Section 2(a), which bars Licensee from using the Marks outside the Morton Territories except for promotion and broadcasting, and with the Internet sales rules in Section 2(b)(v). The instrument does not say how the web right and the territorial limit interact.

'Both parties agree to include links to the other party's Web pages' specifies no placement, prominence, number or duration, so what performance satisfies the promise is indeterminate. A dispute would turn entirely on filling that gap.

A licence 'granted in perpetuity' with no termination clause cannot easily be reconciled with Section 16, which provides for provisions surviving 'the termination of this Agreement', or with Section 3(b)'s reference to 'the Term of this Agreement or thereafter'. Whether the Agreement is terminable at all is left open.

'Licensee shall be solely entitled to all economic benefits' resulting from the licensed rights overlaps Section 3(a)'s reservation of all rights not specifically granted and Section 3(c)'s statement that goodwill inures to Licensor's sole benefit. The scope of the word 'solely' in each is contestable.

'All or substantially all of his assets and/or rights in connection with the use and exploitation of' the Marks sets no threshold, and the duty is only to 'initiate negotiations and to negotiate in good faith' with no price or terms mechanism. Both the trigger and the obligation would have to be construed.

The first-offer right can be circumvented under Section 10, which lets Licensee 'sublicense or franchise any or all of the rights and licenses granted hereunder' without notice to or negotiation with Licensor. Read together, Licensee could transfer the economic substance of the licence without ever triggering 9(c).

'Any or all of the rights and licenses granted hereunder' is unqualified — no consent, no standards for sublicensees, no limit on the number or duration. Whether it permits a transfer of the entire licence in substance is contestable.

An unrestricted sublicensing right can nullify Section 9(c)'s first-offer rights and sits awkwardly with Section 3(a)'s reservation of rights and Licensor's quality-control apparatus in Section 4, which reaches Licensee rather than its sublicensees. The balance of the section (requiring sublicensees to assume Licensee's obligations) mitigates but does not remove the tension.

The promise of court injunctions 'from a court of competent jurisdiction' for breach of 'the terms of this Agreement' overlaps Section 5(a), which commits quality-control disputes to binding arbitration, and Section 5(b), which gives the arbitrator permanent injunctive power. Which route governs a quality-control breach is not stated.

Notices to 'Licensor' are directed to Hard Rock Cafe International (DEL), Inc., although the Licensor named in the preamble and defined in Section 1(n) is Rank Licensing, Inc. A party could argue about who must be served for a notice to be effective.

The flat prohibition that 'Licensee shall not use the name or credit of Licensor in any manner whatsoever' cannot be taken literally alongside the licence in Section 2(a) to use and exploit the Hard Rock Hotel and Casino Marks. The clause carves out only Section 2(b)(iii) for the agency point, not the name point.

The carve-out 'except as provided in Section 5' incorporates the arbitration boundary, so the forum clause is only as determinate as Section 5(a)'s undefined 'provision of quality control' and Section 5(d)'s exclusions. Any forum fight would be resolved by construing those clauses rather than this one.

The survival clause presupposes that the Agreement can terminate, while Section 9(a) makes the licence perpetual and the instrument contains no termination mechanism at all. The clause has no evident field of operation.

The integration clause incorporates 'the Purchase and Sale Agreement', a document neither defined, dated nor attached, so the boundary of the integrated whole is uncertain. It also limits integration to matters 'with respect to the licensing of' the Marks while purporting to supersede prior agreements generally.

Section 19 warrants only power to execute and perform, while the recital states that Licensor 'has the right and authority to license' the Marks and Section 2(a) gives a qualified ownership warranty. The three statements of Licensor's authority are not aligned.

The representation is given about 'the Morton Parties or the Rank Parties', terms that appear nowhere else in this Agreement and are nowhere defined; the parties here are Rank Licensing, Inc. and Peter A. Morton individually. Who is covered by the representation therefore cannot be determined from the instrument.

The clause says the Agreement may be 'amended, supplemented or interpreted at any time only by written instrument duly executed by each of the parties' — making 'interpreted' subject to a formality requirement is anomalous and could be read as an attempt to displace ordinary construction. The word does real, and odd, work in an otherwise standard clause.
